name: Pheochromocytoma

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guidelines for Pheochromocytoma/Paraganglioma

criteria.description: Elevated plasma free metanephrines (metanephrine and/or normetanephrine) >2x upper limit of normal
Adrenal mass identified on cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI)
Histopathological confirmation of chromaffin cell tumor after surgical resection
Positive functional imaging (MIBG scan, 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT, or 18F-FDG PET)
Elevated 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines and catecholamines
Classic triad of episodic headache, sweating, and tachycardia with hypertension

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Biochemical evidence of catecholamine excess (elevated plasma metanephrines) plus anatomic localization by imaging. Definitive diagnosis by histopathology after resection.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Up to 40% of pheochromocytomas are associated with germline mutations. The 'rule of 10s' (10% bilateral, 10% extra-adrenal, 10% malignant, 10% familial) is now considered outdated as hereditary rates are closer to 30-40%.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Classic triad: episodic headache, sweating, and palpitations with hypertension
pathognomonic.notes: Full triad present in ~50%; individual symptoms more common

common.notes: Can be paroxysmal, sustained, or both; orthostatic hypotension also possible

common.symptomName: Anxiety and sense of impending doom

occasional.notes: Due to catecholamine-mediated vasoconstriction; flushing is rare
Paradoxical finding due to chronic catecholamine-induced volume contraction

rare.notes: Can be triggered by surgery, anesthesia, or certain medications

laboratory: Elevated 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines and catecholamines
Elevated plasma or urinary normetanephrine (norepinephrine-secreting) or metanephrine (epinephrine-secreting)
imaging: CT abdomen with contrast showing adrenal mass (typically >3 cm, heterogeneous, >10 HU)
MRI showing characteristic T2 hyperintensity ('light bulb sign')
18F-FDG PET/CT for SDH-related or metastatic pheochromocytoma
genetic: Susceptibility genes: RET (MEN2), VHL, SDHB/C/D, NF1, TMEM127, MAX, FH
SDHB mutations associated with higher malignancy risk
Genetic testing recommended for all patients
other: Clonidine suppression test if biochemical results equivocal
Histopathology: Zellballen pattern, positive chromogranin and synaptophysin staining
PASS (Pheochromocytoma of the Adrenal Gland Scaled Score) for malignancy risk assessment

distinguishingFeatures: Carcinoid features flushing rather than pallor
Thyrotoxicosis has suppressed TSH and elevated free T4
Thyrotoxicosis features weight loss with increased appetite
Heat intolerance more prominent in thyrotoxicosis

redFlags: Hypertensive crisis during surgery or anesthesia (undiagnosed pheochromocytoma)
Paradoxical hypertensive response to beta-blockers (unopposed alpha stimulation)
SDHB mutation carrier (high risk of malignant disease)
Large tumor (>5 cm) or extra-adrenal location (higher malignancy risk)
Family history of MEN2, VHL, NF1, or hereditary paraganglioma syndromes
references: Lenders JW, et al. Pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma: an Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2014;99(6):1915-42.
Neumann HPH, et al. Pheochromocytoma and Paraganglioma. N Engl J Med. 2019;381(6):552-565.
Eisenhofer G, et al. Biochemical diagnosis of pheochromocytoma. Best Pract Res Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2003;17(1):53-73.
Fishbein L, Nathanson KL. Pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma: understanding the complexities of the genetic background. Cancer Genet. 2012;205(1-2):1-11.
